”, Eurobarometer, October, Brussels. The European Investment Bank Investment Report reports similar adoption rates: 46 per cent of EU firms used big data analytics or AI in 2025, and 49 per cent used digital platforms (European Investment Bank (2026), “

Among firms planning AI-related investment over the next 12 months, most expect to invest in AI-related technologies and tools, as well as in employee training, financed mostly through internal funds. 49 per cent of firms plan to invest in AI technologies and tools (e.g. software licences), 46 per cent in training employees, 40 per cent in data and infrastructure and 12 per cent in hiring AI specialists. SPEECH
Next-day securities settlement, tokenisation and the transformation of Europe’s financial infrastructure
Keynote address by Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at an EU T+1 Industry Committee event on “One year to T+1”
Frankfurt am Main, 29 October 2026
We are approaching an important milestone.
[
1
]
Less than a year from now, on 11 October 2027, Europe will move to T+1 settlement. This means that the time from the moment a security is traded to the moment the buyer receives it and the seller is paid will be reduced from two days to one.
This may sound like a technical change, but it is in fact much more significant.
The transition to T+1 is part of a broader transformation of Europe’s financial infrastructure. And the objective is clear: to make Europe’s financial and payment system more efficient, more resilient and safer, and ultimately to make European financial markets more competitive.
In the Eurosystem, we are contributing to this transformation across the full spectrum of our mandate.
We are ensuring that banknotes remain available and fit for purpose. We are preparing for a digital euro. We are modernising wholesale payments and securities settlement. And we are working to enhance cross-border payments and harness new technologies such as distributed ledger technology (DLT).
[
2
]
These are not separate projects. They are different parts of the same strategy: ensuring that the euro and Europe’s financial markets are fit for the future in a rapidly changing world.
From T+2 to T+1: an essential element of a broader modernisation effort
The move to T+1 contributes to this broader strategy.
It is about more than just reducing the time between trade and settlement to one day.
A shorter settlement cycle can reduce market and counterparty risk.
But, perhaps even more importantly for Europe, the transition is also forcing us to review our post-trade processes. It requires greater standardisation, automation and innovation. Inefficiencies that could be accommodated in a T+2 environment will become much more difficult to sustain under T+1.
In that sense, T+1 is a catalyst for modernising European post-trade markets. And this is important for Europe’s competitiveness.
Efficient post-trade infrastructure makes it easier for capital to flow across borders. It helps investors access European markets. And it supports the EU’s wider ambition to create deeper and more integrated capital markets.
It also ensures that Europe keeps pace internationally with other major markets as they shorten their own settlement cycles.
That is why the ECB, together with the European Securities and Markets Authority and the European Commission, strongly supports the market’s preparations for T+1.
There is another lesson for Europe here which I believe is particularly important: we can deliver when we work together.
Europe’s financial landscape remains complex and fragmented. Yet the work coordinated by the EU T+1 Industry Committee has shown that those differences do not need to stand in the way of common solutions.
I would therefore like to congratulate everyone involved for the progress made so far. It is a powerful reminder of what Europe can achieve when public authorities and the private sector come together around a common objective.
But we have not yet crossed the finish line.
The coming months will be critical. Implementation and testing need to advance with the same determination and cooperation that have been the driving force behind the project so far.
The Eurosystem is also responsible for operating TARGET2-Securities (T2S), our platform for securities settlement in central bank money through which cash and securities can be exchanged simultaneously across Europe.
[
3
]
And the key message here is a simple one: T2S already supports shorter settlement cycles. It already settles substantial volumes of transactions on a T+1 and even a T+0 basis.
So we are not starting from scratch.
At the same time, we are adapting some T2S processes to help the market operate efficiently under the tighter timetable that T+1 will bring. This includes changes to the night-time settlement process, which are planned for June 2027 ahead of the market’s migration to T+1 settlement in October 2027.
We will continue working closely with market participants and other European authorities to ensure that the transition to T+1 settlement goes smoothly.
Preparing for the financial system of tomorrow
But while we prepare for T+1, we also need to look further ahead.
Technology is reshaping finance. Distributed ledger technology and tokenisation offer opportunities not only to make today’s processes faster by enabling the near-instant transfer of securities, but potentially to simplify the architecture of finance itself. Tokenisation could bring issuance, trading, clearing, settlement, custody and asset servicing into a shared digital environment.
The Eurosystem intends to be part of that transformation, and we have already moved from vision to delivery.
[
4
]
Since 30 March, the Eurosystem has been accepting marketable assets issued in central securities depositories using distributed ledger technology as eligible collateral for its credit operations.
[
5
]
We are now assessing whether, how and under what criteria DLT-based assets outside currently eligible settlement systems could become eligible collateral. We will ensure that our collateral framework keeps pace with innovation while upholding our statutory requirement for collateral to be adequate.
Since 21 September, Pontes has enabled wholesale transactions in tokenised assets to be settled in central bank money. It connects market DLT platforms with our TARGET Services, bringing the safety of central bank money to the emerging world of tokenised finance.
[
6
]
To further build on this momentum, the Eurosystem will enhance the initial core functionalities of Pontes. We will do so in steps, for example by extending the operating hours significantly by mid-2027 and moving to 24/7/365 availability in 2028. We also plan to offer immediate settlement finality on the Eurosystem DLT platform as early as next year.
Appia looks further ahead.
It is exploring how we can build an integrated European ecosystem for tokenised finance around common standards, with central bank money continuing to provide the anchor of trust and stability.
By 2028, Appia aims to deliver a blueprint setting out key findings, recommendations and principles for a safe, innovative and integrated European tokenised financial ecosystem.
[
7
]
Yesterday we published a report on the outcome of the public consultation on the Appia roadmap.
[
8
]
The consultation confirmed broad market support for developing an integrated, innovative and resilient European tokenised finance ecosystem anchored in central bank money. It also revealed a high degree of willingness among respondents to contribute actively to Appia. This provides a strong basis to develop Appia as a public-private partnership.
But embracing the future does not mean discarding what already works.
So, what does all this mean for T2S?
Let me be very clear: T2S is not going to disappear any time soon.
Different technologies and infrastructures will coexist because they are suited to different functions and different use cases.
T2S will continue to serve European securities markets. At the same time, tokenised platforms will develop and new forms of financial market infrastructure will emerge. The Eurosystem’s tokenisation strategy therefore complements our continuous efforts to improve and modernise our existing TARGET Services.
So we should not frame the discussion as a choice between today’s infrastructure and tomorrow’s technology.
The real challenge is to enable them to coexist.
We need existing and new infrastructures to work together effectively, while preserving the safety of settlement in central bank money and avoiding the emergence of new technological silos.
Innovation should help Europe overcome fragmentation – it shouldn’t recreate that fragmentation in digital form.
Conclusion
Let me conclude.
T+1, T2S, Pontes and Appia may appear to be different initiatives.
But they are connected by a common purpose.
We want Europe’s financial infrastructure to be robust and resilient. We want it to be efficient and innovative. And we want it to provide a foundation on which an integrated and competitive European financial market can develop.
T+1 will be an important step on that journey.
We now have less than a year to complete the transition.
So let us keep up the momentum, intensify implementation and testing, and make Europe’s transition to T+1 a success.
Thank you.

MONETARY POLICY STATEMENT
PRESS CONFERENCE
Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB,
Boris Vujčić, Vice-President of the ECB
Frankfurt am Main, 29 October 2026
Jump to the transcript of the questions and answers
Good afternoon, the Vice-President and I welcome you to our press conference.
The Governing Council today decided to keep the three key ECB interest rates unchanged. Energy prices have continued to rise, posing upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to the growth outlook. While the full effects of the energy shock are still unfolding, underlying inflation has remained broadly stable so far and wages do not show a material response at this stage. The increased magnitude and duration of the energy shock, as well as the implications for indirect and second-round effects, are likely to drive up inflation and lower growth. Financing conditions have tightened since our last meeting, which is likely to weigh on inflation and growth. We are committed to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilises at our two per cent target in the medium term.
We remain well positioned to navigate the current elevated uncertainty. We will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance. In particular, our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data, as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission. We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path.
The decisions taken today are set out in a
press release
available on our website.
I will now outline in more detail how we see the economy and inflation developing and will then explain our assessment of financial and monetary conditions.
Economic activity
The incoming data suggest that the euro area economy continued to expand in the third quarter of the year. Services have recovered, after weakening at the start of the Middle East conflict. Manufacturing, digital services and exports are benefiting from AI-related business investment. Government spending on infrastructure and defence is also supporting activity. These factors should continue to underpin growth in the near term. At the same time, renewed energy price increases have hit consumer confidence, and higher financing costs are likely to weigh on growth.
The unemployment rate remained at 6.4 per cent in August. Growth in employment and the labour force remains subdued, while productivity has gradually picked up.
Over the medium term, a recovery in confidence and real incomes, driven by gradually declining energy prices and a robust labour market, should bolster domestic demand. Investment in AI-related activities and government spending on infrastructure and defence should also continue to support growth. Export growth should pick up on the back of strengthening foreign demand.
Higher potential growth requires structural reform and has to be underpinned by sound public finances. Fiscal sustainability is a crucial anchor for broader economic stability. Fiscal responses to the energy shock should be temporary, targeted and tailored. Simplifying and harmonising rules across the EU’s Single Market, accelerating the energy transition and completing the savings and investments union are key building blocks to make our economy more dynamic and resilient. As the process for agreeing on the legal framework for the digital euro moves into its final stage, we reiterate the importance of reaching agreement on the Single Currency Package as quickly as possible.
Inflation
Inflation rose to 3.8 per cent in September, from 3.2 per cent in August. Energy price inflation increased markedly, to 18.9 per cent, from 14.3 per cent in August. Diesel and petrol prices reached new peaks in September, in part reflecting elevated refining margins. Inflation excluding energy increased to 2.3 per cent in September, from 2.1 per cent in August. Food price inflation increased to 1.3 per cent, from 1.1 per cent. Services inflation increased to 3.2 per cent in September, from 3.0 per cent in August, while goods inflation declined to 1.1 per cent from 1.2 per cent.
Indicators of underlying inflation have remained broadly stable, although the early stages of the pricing chain point to upward pressures. Wage pressures remain moderate. Compensation per employee grew by 3.3 per cent in the second quarter, down from 3.6 per cent in the first quarter, while rising productivity has helped contain the growth of unit labour costs. Our forward-looking wage tracker suggests that negotiated wage growth will fluctuate between 2.5 per cent and 2.8 per cent in the remaining months of 2026 and average 2.6 per cent in the first three quarters of 2027. Inflation expectations over shorter horizons have risen, but most measures of longer-term inflation expectations stand at around 2 per cent, supporting the stabilisation of inflation around target in the medium term.
Energy prices have increased beyond the baseline path foreseen in the September ECB staff projections. This is likely to raise inflation further in the near term and keep headline inflation well above target over the coming quarters. Thereafter, declining energy inflation, together with the effects of higher interest rates, should support the return of inflation to target.
Risk assessment
The risks to the growth outlook are to the downside. This is due, in particular, to the Middle East conflict and recent developments in Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine. Continued disruption of energy supplies could cause energy prices to rise further and for longer than currently expected. This would weigh on real incomes, spending and investment. A worsening of global financial market sentiment or intensifying spillovers in global bond markets could tighten financing conditions and thereby dampen demand. Fiscal uncertainty may also further tighten financing conditions and weaken confidence, thereby lowering consumption and investment. A resurgence of trade tensions between major economies could further disrupt supply chains, reduce exports and weaken consumption and investment. By contrast, growth could turn out to be higher if the economy and energy markets were to adapt more quickly than expected to the disruption caused by the ongoing conflicts or if these were resolved sustainably. Moreover, the adoption of new technologies by euro area firms and government spending on infrastructure and defence, as well as reforms to enhance productivity and complete the EU’s Single Market, may drive up growth by more than expected.
The risks to the inflation outlook are to the upside. This is due, in particular, to the Middle East conflict and recent developments in Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine. The energy shock could intensify further and its effects on other prices and wages could be stronger than currently expected. Gas prices, in particular, could increase if supply is disrupted further or an unusually cold winter coincides with low storage levels. The longer energy prices stay high, the more likely they are to drive up broader inflation through indirect and second-round effects. Renewed trade tensions could give rise to more fragmented global supply chains, curtail the supply of critical raw materials and worsen capacity constraints in the euro area economy. Extreme weather events, potentially reinforced by intensifying “El Niño” conditions, and the unfolding climate and nature crises more broadly, could drive up food prices by more than expected. By contrast, inflation could turn out to be lower if ongoing geopolitical conflicts were resolved sustainably or if indirect or second-round effects from higher energy prices proved less pronounced than anticipated. More volatile and risk-averse financial markets, together with higher long-term interest rates, could weigh on demand and thereby lower inflation as well.
Financial and monetary conditions
Financial conditions have tightened since our previous meeting. Interest rates have broadly moved up, while stock prices have fallen.
The cost of market-based debt for firms rose to 4.1 per cent in August, from 4.0 per cent in July, while bank lending rates for firms remained at 3.8 per cent. Growth in bank lending to firms slowed to an annual rate of 4.2 per cent in August and September, from 4.4 per cent in July, while corporate bond issuance grew at an annual rate of 4.2 per cent in September, up from 3.8 per cent in August and 3.5 per cent in July. Credit standards for loans to firms tightened in the third quarter, as reported in our latest bank lending survey, with banks citing concern about the economic risks faced by their customers. Despite higher financing needs for inventories and working capital, corporate loan demand declined, reflecting in particular higher interest rates.
Mortgage rates rose to 3.6 per cent in August, from 3.5 per cent in July, while mortgage lending growth edged down to 3.0 per cent in September. Credit standards for mortgage lending were unchanged in the third quarter, whereas demand for mortgages declined substantially given higher interest rates.
Conclusion
The Governing Council today decided to keep the three key ECB interest rates unchanged. We are committed to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilises at our two per cent target in the medium term. We will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance. Our interest rate decisions will be based on our assessment of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data, as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission. We are not pre-committing to a particular rate path.
In any case, we stand ready to adjust all of our instruments within our mandate to ensure that inflation stabilises sustainably at our medium-term target and to preserve the smooth functioning of monetary policy transmission.
We are now ready to take your questions.
* * *
The first one, on monetary policy, is that for the first time in I don't know how long the mentioning of second-round effects in your press release was quite striking. So does it also mean that the market is about right to expect a rate hike in December, because clearly there is now a risk of second-round effects?
My second question is: How do you marry your position which was, you said, I think it was spring this year, that the captain stays on the ship when there are clouds on the horizon, given that the euro area is probably in a worse situation than in spring, looking at France, looking at the inflation picture, and perhaps you can tell us more about your motivation?
I would suggest that we deal first and foremost with the monetary policy statement and the monetary policy decision questions, and that if there are additional questions in relation to me, for instance, that we keep that for the end, because the real order of business here is monetary policy. So your second question, I'll deal with it later in the press conference, if that's okay with you.
You are right that second-round effects – and the risk of second-round effects – is something that we have paid very special attention to. I think I said that in previous press conferences. As inflation rises, as the risk to inflation has increased, we pay special attention to the direct effect – we see it clearly – to the indirect effect – we have seen an increase of those indirect effects – and to the secondary effects, which would require a particular policy decision.
We are very attentive and, at this point in time, we are not seeing a risk of second-round effects in addition to what is already included in the projections. So if you will, the projections that were prepared in September did include the risk of second-round effects. So we are looking very attentively to that and, for the moment, as I think we say very clearly in the monetary policy statement, we do not see a material risk of second-round effects at the moment.
But give me the opportunity, because I deferred your second question to a bit later, to give you a little bit of flavour of the debate that we had. Because while we were very attentive to second-round effects, and in particular to the evolution of wages, to the wage tracker, to the compensation per employee projections, to every instrument that we have to measure wages in all sectors, including the opening position of unions in the coming collective bargaining agreement discussions, we have also looked at what has really significantly changed compared to last September.
And the two key changes that we have seen is, first and foremost, the energy prices. And on that front, it's a combination of oil prices, but more importantly, petrol, fuel, gas, and of course refining margins. And that has increased significantly, it's well reflected in the energy inflation numbers – 18.9
[
1
]
if I recall, as compared to a lower number in August
[
2
]
– so a clear increase there.
But another new development that we have observed as well since September is the cost of long-term financing, which has indeed increased. And of course, we look at numbers. And the average 10-year sovereign yields have risen by around 35 basis points since our last cut-off for the September projections.
If you combine these two factors – actually, the Governing Council debated whether a hike was appropriate – but, on the basis of the uncertainty that accumulates and that rises as well, on the basis of underlying inflation that has broadly remained unchanged, the Governing Council unanimously decided that we were well positioned enough at this stage to hold, and that a measured approach, at this point in time, remained appropriate.
So that's the discussion that we had over the last few hours as well as yesterday afternoon. I think it gives you the flavour of dissecting inflation, as much as we could, and the consequences of inflation on wages in particular, but also the overall changes that we have seen, and always applying our three-pronged approach to our monetary policy stance.
Given what you said about upside risk to inflation, you just said the middle path seems appropriate. Was there also consensus on this in the Governing Council? Because you mentioned there was a discussion of raising interest rates. So was there unanimity on this as well, and given this upside risk, do you think the ECB will need to keep raising interest rates at some point in the future?
Second question is why would you leave Europe's most powerful financial position? And I'm especially interested in this thought that you might want to take a greater view on French politics, want to have the ability to express yourself. Is this indeed the case, and in what way would you be doing this? Would you be standing for office, or would you be just commenting on what's happening?
The second question, I will address it at a later stage.
But on your first question, there was that debate. We look at numbers, we look at increased risk, we look at the financial tightening as a result of the long-term interest rates, and pros and cons, and there were views along the lines of maybe now, why not? There was a unanimous decision at the end of the discussion that we were in a sufficiently good position to actually wait for additional information, and the inter-meeting period will be information-rich.
I'm going to take you through the list of what we're going to receive in the next few weeks that will actually help us determine whether the situation that we see now – which could have warranted a hike – is going to be confirmed. And in that case, the sense of direction is quite clear.
So, the list of information that we will have: A new set of staff projections – December will be a projection exercise. Two new inflation prints. Quarter three GDP. Q3 employment, compensation per employee and negotiated wages. Two unemployment readings. Two industrial production releases. The November PMIs. Two rounds of bank interest rate statistics for both September and October.
So as you see, there is a mine of information and data that we will receive in the weeks to come, and this will be particularly relevant with underlying inflation. Because while underlying inflation has not been very informative at the beginning of the shock, the more we progress into the shock, the more informative-rich the underlying inflation indicators are. They are beginning to be more informative and, broadly, they haven't changed. There's a specific mention to that effect in the monetary policy statement.
But with those six weeks of additional information, we will have a lot more in relation to underlying inflation, and that's what we will be particularly attentive to. Not to the detriment on inflation outlook. We will continue to look at the inflation outlook. We will continue to look at the risks. We will most likely produce scenarios again in December. And we will, of course, look at the dynamics and the strength of monetary policy transmission. But underlying inflation will probably take a particular standing in the three-pronged approach that we apply to our monetary policy decision.
My first question is on the French bond markets in particular. So with the kind of spread widening we've seen in recent weeks, there's been a lot of questions about whether and when the ECB should get involved. Can you tell us a bit about which metrics you're watching specifically? Is it more about the speed of the adjustment, the absolute level of the spread, or is it actually about contagion to other countries?
My second question, also in the same vein as my colleagues: I'm sorry about your departure. You're now leaving at the beginning of a year with a lot of national elections, especially in your home country. Did you consider whether this particular timing could undermine the independence of the ECB?
The first response that I would give you is that this long term – and we look at the tenure, we look at the entire curve, but say the long end of the curve across the world, not specifically for a member state, not specifically for the whole of Europe, but across the world – has risen significantly. If you compare numbers, say you take February and now, you have a significant number of basis points that these government
[
3
]
bonds have increased by.
And this is caused by multiple factors. This is caused by expected inflation, this is caused by the expected interest rate path, and we think – and there is a very interesting blog that I highly recommend – we think that the debt issuance by some of the hyperscalers, without really crowding out yet, but increasing the volume of long-term bonds, also plays a role. But that has affected the entire market.
Second observation, and that applies also to all countries: Those countries with high debt have to factor into their fiscal policy plans the fact that interest rates are higher, and will probably remain higher, for a period of time.
In Europe, if you apply that principle, what it means is that policy measures have to be adopted, as part of a plan that is always submitted to Brussels, and that has to comply with the European fiscal framework.
So we will be looking at all that, obviously, and some member states face particular challenges. I would say that it narrows down to those countries that have a high level of debt in general.
But I would also add that, should market developments threaten the smooth transmission of our monetary policy, including through unwarranted and disorderly market movements, we have instruments available to respond. And the criteria and conditions under which this applies are well known, they are published, and I'm sure you know them.
You mentioned that you are still in the phase of measured tightening. That said, why would there be any doubt that the ECB will stick to the quarterly pace and hike again in December?
And my second question, also on a personal note: Will you let us know what you are going to do explicitly after 7 February?
Yes, at this point in time we are still on this measured response to the current situation. And as I said earlier on, we will assess the development of the geopolitical situation, the development of energy prices, the development of tightening of the cost of financing, and any other figures that are relevant to compare the situation as we have it now with what we receive next December. And as I said, unless there was a major development, the direction of travel is quite clear for all of us.
Is there a case for reducing our activity to the quarterly meetings? No. We have never restricted ourselves to that. It is true that we are more data-rich at those projection meetings, but we are also capable of understanding what staff is explaining to us, the information they're collecting, the analysis that they do, and if it was so warranted in order to reach our target of 2% medium-term, not restricted to quarterly meetings. And we have no plan to restrict the number of meetings that will deal with monetary policy.
I have also one on implications of your decision today. So, you are the eighth of 26 Executive Board members in the history of the ECB who is leaving early, before serving the full term, which is quite a high rate. Does this suggest there are flaws in the ECB's governance, or are eight years too long? You said in this Bloomberg interview, early at the start of the year, you initially thought it's a five-year term. So I would be interested in your thoughts on that.
And also, coming back to French bond yields: To what extent is the recent rise in government bond yields doing some of the ECB's work at the moment? And is the need for further interest rates increases reduced because of that?
On your first question, I will only address the issue of governance. I think the governance of the ECB has proven its solidity. We have had transition in the past. Business continuity has always been the mantra for this institution. It has never failed. And I have every confidence that it will continue to apply the principles of continuity, of mission-focused, determined action to reach the target of our 2% medium term. And you can rest assured that until 7 February I'm in charge, I'm focused and I will be working without any reservation, without any excuses.
On your other question, I think I've addressed that, and it's really one of the phenomenons that we have observed which have changed the picture since September. Because yes, you're right, long-term yields have increased across the board. More so in some countries, less so in others, and then you begin looking at the spreads, and we look at everything.
But that has been a qualifying element, if you will, to the increase in energy prices. So energy prices have increased inflation, long-term financing costs have qualified the magnitude of that increase, and it's in those circumstances – which we will be very attentive to in the weeks to come, and with another special focus on underlying inflation – that we will make our decision in December.
I would like to know if this no-hiking thing, because of tighter financial conditions in the markets, is one thing only for this meeting, or if it will happen to continue throughout November, the ECB could not hike or keep interest rates unchanged again because of that?
And a second question for the pile for later. The mandates in the European Council and the European Parliament are going to be discussed before you leave. Would you be interested at all in applying to those positions, just to keep you near?
I think you're right to actually characterise our decision. I hadn't thought about it, but you're right in characterising it as a “no-hiking decision”. Because we did ask ourselves the question, and there was a number of us assessing and pondering whether it was warranted as of now already or whether we needed to confront the current assessment with future data, numbers, elements that we would assess against our three-pronged monetary policy reaction function.
As I have said, and you're probably getting tired of me saying it, but we decide meeting by meeting. So it does not indicate that we will not be hiking and our next meeting is in December. As I've said earlier, I think in response to a previous question, if the assessment that we have today is not infirmed by significant developments, the direction of travel is clear.
I have a question linked to France, and it's only for the second and last part of the answering of the bunch of questions we had today. What really concerns you the most in France, in your home country, and certainly not only the high yields for the moment? So could you maybe describe what are the main concerns? You don't want to stay neutral toward this situation – what will be the nature of your intervention? Do you intend to support actively maybe one candidate or, if so, which one?
And the last, maybe very léger, question is when did you inform your grandchildren about your decision? Je m'en souviens.
Eux aussi. Eux aussi.
Are there other questions on monetary policy?
I was wondering also about France a bit, so it's a bit on the fence of monetary policy. But given the current situation in France, besides the spreads rising, not all that much has changed in the last six months. High debt has been known for quite some time. Yet now there are some talks about the possibility of another euro crisis. I was wondering what your thoughts are on that?
And I do have a second question, also about your departure. Now in the first six months of 2027, three experienced board members will leave the ECB. I was wondering how you will think about the continuity of the ECB in that regard?
So, have there been changes in the last six months? Well, there clearly have been changes. There are the ones that apply to all countries, the ones related to energy prices in general, the ones related to financing – and particularly the financing costs at the long end of the curve, and obviously we are mindful of all such developments.
Do I fear that there will be developments coming up? There will be developments, obviously. But this is not going to deter us, European Central Bank, from delivering on our mission of price stability. And we will continue to do that, on the basis of all the information that we receive.
Two questions, if I may. The first one is what worries you the most today, if it's inflation or financial fragmentation?
And in September, French sovereign bond holdings declined significantly less than Italians and Germans under the quantitative tightening program. So, has the pattern continued in October, and is this purely a mechanical roll-off?
What worries me most is anything that affects price stability, because we are fixated on our mandate, and price stability is our compass. Obviously, inflation matters a lot, but price stability does not take place without financial stability, so we have to look out for any threats to financial stability and any threat to price stability. So, I would say that I would package this too, because what's driving us is the price stability mandate that we have.
Regarding the second question: My understanding of that – but I'm not the top-notch expert for all redemptions of all bonds coming up for all countries across the Member States – what I can tell you is that we are not changing our policy as far as letting redemptions take place without purchasing and without replacing those bonds that come for redemption.
I also know for a fact, but that's from previous life, that November is a pretty heavy month when it comes to France in particular. But it's all mechanical. There is no behind-the-scene arrangement to tweak here, tweak there, rebalance and cut corners. We just apply the principle of no redemption.
Would you like to address the other questions?
Allow me not to necessarily dig into each and every specific aspect of your questions in relation to my decision to step down.
My decision is to step down from my position as President of the European Central Bank after the February monetary policy Governing Council.
So you will have the great pleasure, and I will have the great pleasure, of seeing those of you who care to come twice: once in December, once in February. So we are not done. We will continue to see each other, and I'm delighted about that.
There is never a good time to leave, but it's embedded in the governance of the ECB that presidents, board members, have to leave, because they cannot be up for renewal. So the end of my term in any event would have been October 2027.
The reason I'm anticipating the end of my term, by leaving in February of 2027 instead of October is, as I have said to colleagues, members of staff and governors, because I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters.
As you all know, as President of the European Central Bank – and my colleagues on the Executive Boards and on the Governing Council are under pretty much the same constraints – we have an obligation of neutrality. We comment on the situation with a focus on monetary policy. We are driven by one mandate, and we don't get out of that mandate because that's the price we pay for being independent.
At this time, in relation to many corners of the world – not just European corners, not just Europe – I think that my voice can help, my action can help in relation to principles that are dear to my heart.
One of those principles, because I don't think that I can remain neutral. I don't think that I can be comfortable in that neutrality at the present time. And I'm interested in the truth, and I see the truth being very often damaged, contradicted by misrepresentation, and from the position that I have had for the last 20 plus years of my life, in economic and financial matters, on the international scene as Managing Director of the IMF, as President of the ECB, there are things that I can say. Whether people will listen or not is another story, but I feel that I should say those things, and I cannot do so in my current position. Voilà.
One more thing that I would like to say: I will be replaced, so rest assured that not only the ECB is going to carry on with perfect continuity of business. A process has already started to identify my successor. There are plenty of excellent candidates, much better than me, actually. So don't worry about continuity of business. Don't worry about decision making in limbo. No, absolutely not. The institution is solid, strong, like a rock, and it will continue being so.

In Boston, Lincolnshire, a supplier of ready meals to Marks & Spencer (M&S) manufactures thousands of portions of spaghetti bolognese to be sent to the retailer's shops in the Republic of Ireland.
Every plastic pallet is meticulously individually tagged with a green-grey label “Eire”.
It has been this way since Brexit.
Every truck full of food sent to European Union countries requires hundreds of pages of forms, checks by vets, expense and delays.
It has cost M&S millions of pounds and is part of that reason the British business shut down 11 French stores in 2021.
Many smaller exporters stopped sending their goods to the EU entirely. Some produce, including sausages and certain types of seafood, were entirely stopped.
All this was the predictable consequence of former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s 2020 deal prioritising regulatory freedom over freeflowing goods trade.
That will end with a Brexit "reset" that Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign with the EU on Friday.
The government claims it could boost the economy to the tune of £5bn a year and cut the cost of food for households.
But will the agreement mean a return to frictionless trade for food with the EU or are there trade-offs and quid pro quos the UK will have to make?
EU affairs minister Hamish Falconer, who is a key negotiator with the bloc,  acknowledged a “choice” is being made.
In exchange for being able to export produce such as Lincolnshire sausages to the 27 countries, the flipside is the extent to which the UK will be able to influence EU food policies.
The UK will have a "voice in the room", said Falconer, but no vote. Critics have said a reset will make the UK "a rule taker", not a rule maker.
But Falconer said the UK will be involved in a process to shape the rules.
Exit clause
A Brexit reset would not involve any upfront payments, said Falconer, but made it clear there could well be an "exit clause" in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment.
He said this was "reasonable" to consider what would happen if a future Conservative or Reform government wanted to undo the new arrangements. Both parties have said they would  if they were in power.
"The EU is worried about that and you can see why," he said.
The BBC understands that the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place following Brexit.
The reset means they will be dismantled.
Image source,
Getty Images
The prime minister has said
he believes there is a "win-win" deal
to be had with the EU.
Speaking at a Marks & Spencer food court in central London, Falconer said reducing the cost of importing food "will mean less cost for supermarkets, and I hope that less cost then turns into cheaper produce on the shelves".
He said companies have to currently deal with "pages and pages" of form-filling.
Some exports are rejected for having the wrong colour of ink on forms, or an inaccurate Latin name for cooked meats.
The reset could also mean "tearing up" checks that were introduced on goods flowing from Great Britain to Northern Ireland, following Brexit, he said, as well as separate "Not for EU" labelling.
The whole deal to be signed on Friday is calculated to add 0.4% to UK GDP.
Image source,
Marcin Nowak/Anadolu via Getty Images
Image caption,
Minister for EU relations Hamish Falconer
Tom Bradshaw, president of the National Farmers' Union, welcomed reduced border inspections and paperwork but said that for the NFU it was "a moment of opportunity and risk" with farmers waiting to see what carve-outs and transitional arrangements would be included.
Trade volumes in food exports to the EU had "fallen significantly - by over a third" since 2019, he said.
But the UK should take a "pragmatic" approach to implementing any new rules.
He raised pesticides and precision breeding - or gene edited crops - as areas where he hoped some compromise would be found.
UK firms are, for example, developing tomatoes engineered to contain extra vitamin D.
Historically the EU has had much stricter rules on gene-editing, but this year relaxed regulations.
Falconer said people would have to "wait and see the detail" in this area.
Contentious crisp flavourings
Another contentious area has been crisp flavourings, with concerns raised that stricter EU rules on certain ingredients might limit the sale of some popular snack flavours in the UK.
"I want to take this opportunity to absolutely stamp down on misinformation about smoky bacon crisps," Falconer said.
Post-Brexit the UK had stayed "pretty closely aligned" to European food safety standards, he said.
Two leading snack brands had already adapted their recipes to accommodate EU rules, an example of the kind of alignment that would happen whether or not there was a reset of UK-EU relations.
"The truth is, almost every business in this country that wants to export food or drink will be aligning with EU rules because it's our biggest market.
"Lots of people, like the good people at Walkers and Frazzles have made these changes already, so I would want to reassure people, particularly smoky bacon fans, it's okay," he said.

It's easy to see the appeal of a beauty advent calendar. Like many women at this time of year, Julia says she often finds herself tempted to splurge on one - especially a perfume calendar. But she takes quite an unsentimental approach.
"I always look at what's in them. If I like enough of the fragrances, I'll buy it," says the 39-year old, who works as a senior commercial manager in engineering.
Luxury advent calendars are supposed to offer the thrill of a surprise but, for Julia, it is more important she actually wants the items inside - a thought that is also striking more and more customers in the wake of the scandal over the Skims calendar.

High-profile brands will warn that their calendars risk running out, which may boost early demand, while unboxing videos posted by influencers can encourage spending by creating an infectious sense of surprise and delight.
And it appears to be working.

A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.
On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.
For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.
With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.
But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.
Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.
Megaspeed is a case in point.
It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
The city-state has had some success in policing this.
It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.
They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.
Image source,
AFP via Getty Images
Image caption,
Megaspeed's office in Singapore
In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.
The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.
Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.
But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.
Singapore authorities said they had also investigated
Alice Huang
- not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.
In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.
Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.
Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.
In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.
Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.
Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity.
On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".
China has also long rebuffed accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.
Image source,
Reuters
Image caption,
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following a board meeting
How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.
In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely
views China positively.
For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.
But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.
Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.
BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.
In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.
Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man.
During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.
Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.
Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.
Image source,
Reuters
Image caption,
Alice Huang, seen here in Taipei with Jensen Huang last year, ran Megaspeed for several months in 2023
All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore.
"For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.
Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".
But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.
With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.
Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said.
"Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.
But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China".
"This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."

Monetary policy decisions
29 October 2026
The Governing Council today decided to keep the three key ECB interest rates unchanged. Energy prices have continued to rise, posing upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to the growth outlook. While the full effects of the energy shock are still unfolding, underlying inflation has remained broadly stable so far and wages do not show a material response at this stage. The increased magnitude and duration of the energy shock, as well as the implications for indirect and second-round effects, are likely to drive up inflation and lower growth. Financing conditions have tightened since the Governing Council’s last meeting, which is likely to weigh on inflation and growth. The Governing Council is committed to setting monetary policy to ensure that inflation stabilises at its 2% target in the medium term.
The Governing Council remains well positioned to navigate the current elevated uncertainty. It will follow a data-dependent and meeting-by-meeting approach to determining the appropriate monetary policy stance. In particular, the Governing Council’s interest rate decisions will be based on its assessment of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data, as well as the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission. The Governing Council is not pre-committing to a particular rate path.
Key ECB interest rates
The interest rates on the deposit facility, the main refinancing operations and the marginal lending facility will remain unchanged at 2.50%, 2.65% and 2.90% respectively.
Asset purchase programme (APP) and pandemic emergency purchase programme (PEPP)
The APP and PEPP portfolios are declining at a measured and predictable pace, as the Eurosystem no longer reinvests the principal payments from maturing securities.
***
The Governing Council stands ready to adjust all of its instruments within its mandate to ensure that inflation stabilises at its 2% target in the medium term and to preserve the smooth functioning of monetary policy transmission. Moreover, the Transmission Protection Instrument is available to counter unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics that pose a serious threat to the transmission of monetary policy across all euro area countries, thus allowing the Governing Council to more effectively deliver on its price stability mandate.
The President of the ECB will comment on the considerations underlying these decisions at a press conference starting at 14:45 CET today.

Have you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person?
Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw.
From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place.
But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing".
So how much AI enhancement is too much?
'The rooms were much smaller'
Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye.
But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place.
"The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different."
For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison.
Image source,
Winkworth/Supplied
Image caption,
AI has been used to make the property look more luxurious
It later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI.
But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time.
"It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for."
All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down.
'A surge of AI listings'
Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible.
It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly.
According to a recent survey
,
external
of 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was.
Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months.
He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential.
But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time.
"I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person."
He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated.
Image source,
Howards/Supplied
Image caption,
Cara says AI was used to empty her son's room in the image on the left
Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove.
In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter.
In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down.
Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing.
"If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says.
Image source,
Howards/Supplied
Image caption,
In one picture (l), the AI removed a doll's house and changed the shape of a rug
A spokeswoman told the BBC that Howards had now introduced a policy of labelling all AI-enhanced photos. She added that the firm never used AI "to misrepresent the fundamental features of a property".
"It's about helping people imagine the possibilities, not changing the reality of what's being sold."
'Jumping on the bandwagon'
Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology.
But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.
Jack Bushrod thinks all estate agents should have to clearly label AI-enhanced photos and mention any use of the tech prominently in the key features slide of a property listing.
He also expects to see more housefishing as time goes on.
"My worry is the more estate agents use AI, others will see the trend and jump on the bandwagon."

Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
The loss-making company says it will offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each and will raise up to $64bn when it floats this month.
It would value Anthropic at between $1.1tn and $1.3tn which, although large, is below the $2tn some backers of the firm predicted in summer, according to the Financial Times.
The huge valuation comes despite the company warning last month that
AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity".
It is floating at a volatile time for big tech firms. After last week's US midterm elections, the Nasdaq fell sharply on concerns a Democrat-led Congress could slow development of AI and the buildout of data centres.
There are also wider fears over the billions of dollars being spent on AI and whether it will pay off.
In its most recent results for the six months to the end of June, Anthropic's revenues jumped to $16.2bn from $1.1bn in the same period last year.
However, its pre-tax loss jumped to $80.7bn from $12.9bn.
Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, said the $64bn Anthropic wants to raise is "fairly bullish" within "the volatility [and] concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week".
She told Reuters: "It's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there."
Anthropic, which will list under the symbol ANT on 19 November, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.
At $1.3tn, Anthropic's possible valuation is below SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company, which listed its shares in June and was valued at nearly $1.8tn.

Kim Kardashian's Skims is offering customers refunds for its $148 (£110) advent calendar which has been widely criticised on social media.
The accessories advent calendar promised "twelve days of fun surprises" but has been mocked online for the quality of its contents, such as hair clips and keychains, with some comparing them to something you would find down the back of a sofa.
A spokesperson for Skims has told a number of media outlets "for some, the calendar didn't meet expectations" and the company has "personally contacted every customer" to offer a full refund or credit to put towards other products".
The BBC has contacted Skims for comment.
The shapewear and clothing business was co-founded by Kardashian in 2019 and has made the reality TV star a billionaire, according to Forbes magazine.
Skims was valued at $5bn in 2025 when it raised millions of dollars in new funding.
One account on TikTok called spicychathouse compared the contents of the calendar to things "my cat collects from around my house". Another account said it looked like "a bunch of stuff that Kim Kardashian was emptying out of her bedside table".
A number of accounts showed people cleaning out their own sofas and claiming they had accidentally created the Skims advent calendar.
"It is really interesting to see this kind of backlash," said Kate Vlietstra, senior director of food and drink at market research analyst Mintel.
"It is something we have been seeing a bit more in recent years, particularly with the trend for unboxing on social media," she said,
"It means that, inevitably, if people are not feeling they're getting the value that they have hoped for from the advent calendar...they've purchased, then yes, there is going to be a backlash."
Advent calendars remain popular, according to Helen Wing, head of innovation at market research company Ipsos though she said that "the buzz around them has reduced a little bit".
She said according to Ipsos research, people are willing to pay a bit more for an advent calendar but the contents have to justify the price tag.
Using a £285 advent calendar sold by Liberty as an example, Wing said the upmarket department story is "very open about the value of the contents".
"They will say there is over £1,000 worth of content," she said. "If you've got that reassurance when you're making the purchase, particularly if it is for a gift, then it is important to have some faith that the contents are actually going to be worth the money that you're paying."

Sales of essential goods such as bottled water and canned food soared in the 10 days following the launch of the government's "Be Ready" emergency preparedness campaign on 22 October, research indicates.
Hand sanitiser sales were up 83%, sales of bottled water rose 67% and tinned and jarred goods climbed 37%, according to data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator.
The government's
public awareness campaign
encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.
However, Worldpanel said that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.
The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.
Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.
After the campaign launch, the equivalent of an extra 400,000 people per day bought tinned meat, Worldpanel said, although the typical amount remained at 500g, which suggests a gradual stocking-up.
"Shoppers clearly took notice of the 'Be Ready' campaign, but this wasn't panic buying, with less than a third of households buying bottled water in October," said Fraser McKevitt, head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel by Numerator.
"Growth came from more people adding the recommended items on the government's checklist to their weekly shop, not from shoppers piling their trolleys high, which is very much in line with what the government wanted households to do," he said.
Sales of tinned and jarred goods rose from £58.2m in the 10 days to 2 November 2025 to £79.5m over the same period in 2026.
Bottled water sales jumped from £13.6m to £22.8m compared with a year earlier and hand sanitiser sales climbed from £497,000 to £908,000.
Further evidence of stockpiling came from food firm Princes on Tuesday, which said demand for tinned tuna, meat and vegetables had risen following the government's campaign.
Princes interim chief executive Giuseppe Mastrolia said the jump in demand "further reinforces the relevance of our core categories in providing affordable, nutritious and convenient food solutions".
The "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need - for example, bottled water, and long-life food that doesn't need to be kept in the fridge such as dried fruit and nuts.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".
Disaster recovery expert Lucy Easthope previously told the BBC that
the UK was playing "massive catch up" to other European nations
in terms of preparedness.
These include France, Germany Denmark, Sweden, and Norway.
A number of experts have been calling for the UK to put more emphasis on food security, with some arguing that the government itself should take responsibility for food stockpiling, rather than individual households.
In October, a group of more than 180 experts
signed an open letter
,
external
to Burnham and first secretary of state Louise Haigh calling for local authorities to have a duty to prevent and respond to food supply emergencies.
They pointed out that a government survey found that 29% of people in the UK could not afford to keep a few days worth of food in the house.

NAND闪存价格下跌：
美银在一份报告中表示，
自10月中下旬以来，NAND闪存现货价格已下跌约20%
。512 Gb NAND晶圆现货价格报14.30美元，单周下跌12%，较上一季度下跌32%。分析师认为，本轮下跌原因在于：
存储芯片
价格大涨后，PC与手机厂商削减存储配置、减少元器件采购，同时大型云厂商订单回落。NAND厂商抢占市场份额、供应商之间的价格竞争，也对价格形成压制。进一步加剧下行压力的是，全球20%–30%的NAND产能来自老旧产线，这类产能持续面向通用IT市场出货。
美银预计，通用IT领域NAND价格明年一季度还将继续下跌5%–10%
，带动整体平均售价（ASP）小幅走低，这和市场此前预期的涨幅超10%形成反差。一位行业人士表示：“本轮走弱主要集中在手机、PC所用的通用型NAND”，并补充称，AI
数据中心
所用企业级NAND需求依旧强劲。
